\chapter{Asking --- Every Question Begins with K}
\label{ch:sa-asking}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask when, why, how many and from where in Sanskrit, and I can see that every question word is built on one stem.}

Complete SA-C18-k-words and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kadā]{\sk{कदा} (kadā) — when?}

\label{lesson:SA-C18-when}



\begin{quote}
You can say when. This chapter is for asking when.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कदा}}
\textbf{\sk{कदा}} (\emph{kadā}) — \textquotedblleft{}when?\textquotedblright{}

Set it beside the word you just learned and something jumps out:

\emph{\sk{सदा}} — always. \emph{\sk{कदा}} — when?

One letter apart, and the difference is the whole of this chapter. Sanskrit builds its question words on \textbf{\sk{क्}} (\emph{k-}), and it builds several of its answering words on \textbf{\sk{स्}} (\emph{s-}) or \textbf{\sk{त्}} (\emph{t-}). Ask with \emph{k-}, answer with \emph{t-}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Your first \emph{k-} word met deliberately. There are four more in this chapter, and by the end the pattern will be doing the remembering for you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kadā} — \textquotedblleft{}when?\textquotedblright{}
  \item it against its answer — \emph{kadā}, \emph{sadā}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}when does he read?\textquotedblright{} — \emph{kadā paṭhati}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What single letter separates \sk{कदा} from \sk{सदा}? (\emph{K-} against \emph{s-}.) Which letter opens a Sanskrit question word? (\emph{K-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kimartham]{\sk{किमर्थम्} (kimartham) — why?}

\label{lesson:SA-C18-why}



\begin{quote}
The hardest question in any language, and Sanskrit builds it out of two words you can almost read.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{किमर्थम्}}
\textbf{\sk{किमर्थम्}} (\emph{kimartham}) — \textquotedblleft{}why?\textquotedblright{}

It is transparently two pieces:

\emph{\sk{किम्}} (\textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{\sk{अर्थम्}} (\textquotedblleft{}for the purpose of, for the sake of\textquotedblright{})

— literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}for what purpose?\textquotedblright{}} Sanskrit does not have a single opaque word for \emph{why}; it asks what the aim was, and lets the shape of the question show.

\emph{\sk{अर्थ}} (\emph{artha}) is worth keeping on its own. It means purpose, aim, meaning, and wealth all at once, and it is one of the four goals of life in the classical scheme. A word for \textquotedblleft{}why\textquotedblright{} built on it is asking, quite seriously, \emph{what is this for?}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A compound you can take apart on sight — and \emph{k-} again at the front, exactly as promised.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kimartham} — \textquotedblleft{}why?\textquotedblright{}
  \item its two pieces — \emph{kim} and \emph{artham}
  \item what \sk{अर्थ} means on its own (purpose, aim, meaning, wealth)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \sk{किमर्थम्}? (\emph{Kim}, \textquotedblleft{}what,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{artham}, \textquotedblleft{}for the purpose of.\textquotedblright{}) What does \sk{अर्थ} mean by itself? (Purpose, aim, meaning, wealth.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kati]{\sk{कति} (kati) — how many?}

\label{lesson:SA-C18-how-many}



\begin{quote}
You can count to five. This asks how many there are.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कति}}
\textbf{\sk{कति}} (\emph{kati}) — \textquotedblleft{}how many?\textquotedblright{}

\emph{K-} at the front again, and this time the relatives are visible outside Sanskrit too: Latin \emph{quot}, \textquotedblleft{}how many,\textquotedblright{} is the same word, and it survives in English \textbf{quota} and \textbf{quotient} — both of them, at root, answers to \emph{how many}.

Pair it with the numbers you already have and it is immediately useful: \sk{कति} \sk{गृहाणि}, \textquotedblleft{}how many houses?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three \emph{k-} words now, and one of them has handed you two English words as a souvenir.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kati} — \textquotedblleft{}how many?\textquotedblright{}
  \item its Latin cousin — \emph{quot}
  \item the two English words built on it (\emph{quota}, \emph{quotient})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin word is \sk{कति} related to? (\emph{Quot}.) Which English words carry it? (\emph{Quota}, \emph{quotient}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kutaḥ]{\sk{कुतः} (kutaḥ) — from where?}

\label{lesson:SA-C18-from-where}



\begin{quote}
You can ask where something is. This asks where it came from.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कुतः}}
\textbf{\sk{कुतः}} (\emph{kutaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}from where? whence?\textquotedblright{}

You already have \textbf{\sk{कुत्र}} (\emph{kutra}), \textquotedblleft{}where?\textquotedblright{} Now compare the two endings:

\emph{\sk{कुत्र}} — where, at what place. \emph{\sk{कुतः}} — from where, out of what place.

The \emph{-tas} ending means \textquotedblleft{}from,\textquotedblright{} and Sanskrit uses it far beyond question words. English once had this distinction too and has mostly lost it: \emph{where} against \emph{whence}, \emph{there} against \emph{thence}. Sanskrit keeps them working.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four \emph{k-} words, and a distinction English has let go of. When a language keeps a difference yours has dropped, that is worth noticing rather than flattening.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kutaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}from where?\textquotedblright{}
  \item it against \emph{kutra}, \textquotedblleft{}where?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English pair that used to make the same distinction (\emph{where}, \emph{whence})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \emph{-tas} ending add? (\textquotedblleft{}From.\textquotedblright{}) Which English word matches \sk{कुतः}? (\emph{Whence}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ka-śabdāḥ]{\sk{क}-\sk{शब्दाः} (ka-śabdāḥ) — every question begins with k-}

\label{lesson:SA-C18-k-words}



\begin{quote}
Every question word you have met, gathered in one place, so you can see they are one word wearing different endings.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{क}-\sk{शब्दाः}}
Line them up:

\emph{\sk{कः}} — who? · \emph{\sk{किम्}} — what? · \emph{\sk{कुत्र}} — where? · \emph{\sk{कुतः}} — from where? · \emph{\sk{कथम्}} — how? · \emph{\sk{कदा}} — when? · \emph{\sk{कति}} — how many?

Seven questions, one opening consonant. Sanskrit builds them all on a single interrogative stem \textbf{\sk{क}-} and distinguishes them entirely by what follows.

The family reaches much further than Sanskrit. That \emph{k-} is the ancestral \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}-}, which became Latin \emph{qu-} — \emph{quis}, \emph{quid}, \emph{quando}, \emph{quot} — and, by a regular sound change, Germanic \emph{hw-}, which English writes \textbf{wh-}: \emph{who}, \emph{what}, \emph{where}, \emph{when}, \emph{how}.

So \emph{\sk{कः}} and \emph{who}, \emph{\sk{किम्}} and \emph{what}, \emph{\sk{कदा}} and \emph{when} are not lookalikes. They are the same words, separated by five thousand years.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You now hold every basic question in Sanskrit, and one fact that makes them nearly impossible to forget: if it opens with \sk{क्}, it is asking you something.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all seven, in a row
  \item the English \emph{wh-} word for each
  \item what the \emph{k-} became in Latin (\emph{qu-})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do all seven share? (An opening \sk{क्}.) What did that consonant become in Latin, and in English? (\emph{Qu-}, and \emph{wh-}.) Are \sk{कः} and \emph{who} related? (Yes — the same word, five thousand years apart.)
\end{tcolorbox}
